title: Instant Winner on an N-by-N Board
statement:
Two players take cells on an n × n board. A player wins the moment they own every cell of one row, one column, the main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right) or the anti-diagonal (top-right to bottom-left).

  • TicTacToe(n) creates an empty board.
  • move(row, col, player) gives cell (row, col) to player (1 or 2) and returns that player's number if this move wins, otherwise 0.

Every move is to an empty cell, and no moves are made after someone has won. Players do not necessarily alternate. Each call should take less than O(n²) time; O(1) is possible.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the board. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: Player 1 completes the top row with the last move.
Cells (0,1) and (1,0) form the anti-diagonal of a 2×2 board, where row + col = n − 1.

constraints: At most n² calls to move
hints: After a move, only four lines can have just been completed: the move's row, its column, and the two diagonals if the cell is on them.
Checking those four lines costs O(n). To get O(1), stop storing the board and store counts instead.
Keep, per player, a count of cells owned in each row, each column and each diagonal. A move adds one to at most four counters; the player wins when one of them reaches n.

explain.intuition:
A move can only finish a line that passes through it, so the first improvement is to check just that row, that column, and the diagonals the cell lies on. That is O(n) per move.

For O(1), notice you never need the board itself, only "how many cells of this line does this player own". Since cells are never taken twice, those counts only go up, and a line is won when its count hits n. A common trick is one signed counter per line: add +1 for player 1 and −1 for player 2. The line belongs entirely to one player exactly when the counter reaches +n or −n.
steps: Keep arrays rows[n] and cols[n], and two numbers diag and anti, all starting at 0.
On move(r, c, p), let d = p === 1 ? 1 : −1. Add d to rows[r] and cols[c].
If r === c, add d to diag. If r + c === n − 1, add d to anti. (A centre cell is on both.)
If any of those four values now has absolute value n, return p. Otherwise return 0.
pitfalls: Forgetting the anti-diagonal, or testing it with r === n − c instead of r + c === n − 1.
Using else if between the two diagonal updates. On odd boards the centre cell belongs to both.
Checking for a win by scanning the whole board after every move, which is O(n²) per call.

solutions.title: Store the board, check four lines
solutions.idea: Keep the board. After a move, scan only its row, its column, and the diagonals it is on.

solutions.title: Signed counters per line
solutions.idea: Player 1 adds +1 and player 2 adds −1 to the counters of the row, column and diagonals of the move. A counter at ±n means one player owns that whole line.
solutions.py:
class TicTacToe:
    def __init__(self, n: int):
        self.n = n
        self.rows = [0] * n
        self.cols = [0] * n
        self.diag = self.anti = 0

    def move(self, row: int, col: int, player: int) -> int:
        d = 1 if player == 1 else -1
        self.rows[row] += d
        self.cols[col] += d
        if row == col:
            self.diag += d
        if row + col == self.n - 1:  # not "elif": the centre is on both
            self.anti += d
        n = self.n
        if n in (abs(self.rows[row]), abs(self.cols[col]), abs(self.diag), abs(self.anti)):
            return player
        return 0

followups: A player now needs only k in a row (like five-in-a-row on a large board). Do the counters still work?
Add an undo() method that takes back the last move.
